# Does the Kalshi Favorite–Longshot Bias Survive Fees and Publication?

### A replication of Bürgi, Deng & Whelan, with an extension to June 2026

**Draft — 2026-08-27.** Numbers in this note are generated by the pipeline in
`kalshi-makers-takers-persistence` and are reproducible from
`reports/r1/r1_report.json`, `reports/r2/verdict_lock.json` and
`reports/r2/escalation_run.json`. The R2 specification was committed to
`docs/analysis_plan.md` on 2026-07-28, a month before any R2 estimate existed.

---

## Abstract

Bürgi, Deng and Whelan (2026, hereafter BDW) provide the first systematic
evidence on pricing in the Kalshi prediction market, documenting a
favorite–longshot bias and a maker/taker return asymmetry over 2021 to April
2025. They close by inviting exactly one follow-up: whether the patterns
persist now that they have been publicly documented. We take up that
invitation on 376.8 million fills through June 2026.

We reproduce their headline results. All five of their by-year Mincer–Zarnowitz
slopes are recovered with matching sign and significance; the maker margin at
prices ≥50c comes back at +2.09% against their +2.6%, and the maker share of
volume at the two tails at 43.1% and 57.0% against their 43.5% and 56.5%.

We then report three things they could not have known.

First, **the maker fee is not the treatment their sample cutoff implies.**
Sixteen dated captures of Kalshi's own published fee schedule show a per-series
surcharge, revised five times, covering 8.0% to 14.4% of in-scope markets —
never the exchange-wide regime change the paper's framing assumes. It also
began on 2025-05-13, and its first form was flat per contract rather than
quadratic in price.

Second, **on the estimate that identifies, the fee did not move the bias.** A
series-level difference-in-differences comparing treated and untreated series
trading in the same months returns −0.0016 with a standard error of 0.0064 —
a tight null on 1.33 million observations and 119,646 event clusters.

Third, and most consequentially for anyone else who studies this venue,
**41% of the naive aggregate movement at the fee boundary is composition, not
behaviour.** Sports went from 0.009% of the 2024 sample to 58.8% of the
post-boundary sample in fourteen months. A before/after comparison of aggregate
bias on Kalshi measures that arrival, and reports it as an effect.

---

## 1. Introduction

BDW's sample stops in April 2025, and the stopping point is not arbitrary. They
say so themselves: Kalshi "began to charge fees on Makers after April 2025," a
change that taxes the one margin their paper identifies as exploitable — maker
returns of +2.6% on contracts priced at or above 50c. Everything after their
window therefore sits under a treatment aimed squarely at the thing they
measured, and until now nobody had looked.

Their Section 6 makes the invitation explicit:

> We think it will be interesting to see if the biases and return patterns that
> we have reported persist now that they have been publicly documented.

Two features make this answerable rather than merely askable. The maker fee
(May 2025) and the paper's first public posting as CEPR DP 20631 (2025-09-08)
sit roughly four months apart, so a decay that begins at the fee date is priced
cost while a decay that begins at the publication date is the anomaly being
arbitraged away — the McLean–Pontiff post-publication question, asked on a
prediction market rather than a stock cross-section. And the whole thing runs
on historical data from a public API, so it is reproducible by anyone.

The obvious way to answer it is also wrong, and Section 6 of this note is about
why.

## 2. Data and construction

All data come from Kalshi's public `trade-api/v2` endpoints. No account, no
authentication, no order placement. Collection runs in two passes: a
universe-wide pass for market metadata, the eleven boundary trades per contract
that the daily-lookback price panel needs, and closing quotes for the spread
filter; then a full trade-tape pass, restricted to contracts that survive the
filters, because the maker/taker estimands need every fill's price, size and
taker side and boundary ticks cannot substitute.

The finished tape is **376,760,957 fills across 62 monthly partitions**. The R2
in-scope set — markets clearing $1,000 volume, 24 hours open, and a closing
spread at or under 20c — is **392,597 markets**, all of them taped.

Three construction choices are worth stating because each silently changes the
sample.

**Volume.** BDW write "total traded volume at closure ≥ $1,000", which reads as
dollar notional. Kalshi's own `volume` field is denominated in contracts and the
API exposes no notional field. The two readings are nearly indistinguishable in
prose and are not indistinguishable in data: at the contract reading our
independently collected universe lands within 0.1% of their 12,403 events and
2.9% of their 46,282 contracts, so the contract reading is primary. The dollar
reading roughly halves the sample and is retained as a reported branch, because
a sample rule that differentially removes cheap strikes is itself a result in a
paper about the favorite–longshot bias.

**No-trade lookback days.** BDW describe "last trade before the same time on
each of up to 10 prior days", which reads as skipping days with no trade. Their
own arithmetic says otherwise: 156,986 prices over 46,282 contracts is 3.39
prices per contract, and skipping cannot reach it. Measured on our tape,
skipping yields 2.50 per contract and carrying the last price forward yields
3.50 — a 3.2% match against their 3.39 versus 26% low. Carrying forward is
therefore primary and skipping is a reported branch. The distinction is not
cosmetic: under skipping, 6,925 of 32,728 contracts (21.2%) contribute no panel
row at all.

**One construction on both sides of every boundary.** R2 measures a *change* in
the slope within our own data and references our own ψ̄, not BDW's. A
construction that switched at a boundary would be the one thing that actually
breaks identification, so the rule is fixed before any δ is computed. Level
fidelity to BDW is an R1 goal, not an R2 one.

## 3. R1: the reproduction

Counts come before estimates. Divergence on overlapping deterministic data is a
coverage question, not a sampling question, so BDW's standard errors are not
the tolerance and are not used as one.

| | ours | BDW | Δ |
|---|---|---|---|
| Events | 10,061 | 12,403 | −18.9% |
| Yes contracts | 33,222 | 46,282 | −28.2% |
| Yes prices | 124,732 | 156,986 | −20.6% |
| Doubled prices | 249,464 | 313,972 | −20.6% |

The shortfall is dominated by the spread filter. Of the 39,794 markets clearing
volume and duration, 3,257 (8.2%) have a quote row whose spread is null —
Kalshi genuinely serves no bid/ask history for them, so this cannot shrink by
fetching more. Only 11 markets (0.03%) are merely unfetched. BDW did not lose
these, which means their spread filter bit far less than ours; we report the gap
rather than tuning a filter to close it.

**By-year slopes.** The Mincer–Zarnowitz regression `(Y−P) = α + ψP + ε` in
cents, Yes-only, event-clustered:

| Year | ours | s.e. | BDW |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2021 | 0.0409 | 0.0159 | 0.041 |
| 2022 | 0.0202 | 0.0122 | 0.023 |
| 2023 | 0.0217 | 0.0144 | 0.036 |
| 2024 | 0.0386 | 0.0083 | 0.048 |
| 2025 (Jan–Apr) | 0.0171 | 0.0126 | 0.021 |

Every year is positive with a matching significance pattern. Magnitudes run
systematically a little below theirs, all within roughly one standard error.
2021 lands on their value to three decimals on independently collected data.

**The bias itself.** In the 1–10c band, contracts win 2.43% of the time at a
mean price of 3.22c; in the 91–99c band they win 97.86% at a mean price of
97.08c. Cheap contracts win less often than their price implies and expensive
ones more often — BDW's Figure 3, reproduced. Gross returns in the bottom band
are −37.3%, and −49.2% net of their fee model.

**Makers and takers.** This is the part R2 exists to re-test:

| | ours | BDW |
|---|---|---|
| Makers | −1.33% | −9.64% |
| Takers | −28.40% | −31.46% |
| Makers, price ≥50c | **+2.09%** | **+2.6%** |
| Maker share, 1–10c | 43.1% | 43.5% |
| Maker share, 90–99c | 57.0% | 56.5% |

The maker share figures are on the doubled basis, which is the basis BDW state
theirs on, and they match closely. The overall maker return is our one material
divergence and is logged as such rather than explained away.

**Two methodological confirmations.** The specification calls for
Cameron–Gelbach–Miller two-way (event, contract) clustering, and argues it
reduces algebraically to one-way event clustering when contracts nest in events.
Estimated both ways on the real panel, the standard errors agree to fourteen
decimal places (ψ s.e. 0.006003661900808133 versus …132). Separately, Kalshi's
taker-side fields are populated on **100.0%** of all 376,760,957 fills in every
era, with no unparseable timestamps — which upgrades a pre-fetch diagnostic that
had rested on a single market's 152 trades to full-sample evidence.

## 4. What the fee schedule actually says

BDW model Kalshi's fees as a single uniform taker formula, `$0.07·P(1−P)` per
contract rounded up per order, with makers exempt until "after April 2025". We
reconstructed the schedule from **sixteen dated captures of Kalshi's own
published fee document** (2021-07 to 2026-02), plus per-series fee metadata for
all 12,231 series from Kalshi's API. Four findings follow, each load-bearing.

**The maker fee was never exchange-wide.** Resting orders are free, in the
schedule's own words, "unless they are included in our 'Maker Fees' section" —
29 series at introduction, then 39, 48, 101 and 111 by 2025-09-17. On our
in-scope universe that is 8.0% of markets and 61.0% of volume in the first-list
era, rising to 14.4% and 66.2%. A minority of markets, a majority of dollars.

**Its first form was flat.** `round_up(0.0025·C)` per contract, with no price
dependence at all, becoming the quadratic `0.0175·C·P·(1−P)` only on 2025-07-08.

**It began 2025-05-13**, by the document's own "Last Updated" stamp — after
BDW's cutoff, so their statement is confirmed and sharpened.

**Two carve-outs they do not model.** The taker rate was 0.14 in the 2021-07-20
capture, falling to 0.07 on 2021-08-01. And S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 markets pay
half rate, 0.035, in every capture from 2022-09 onward — covering **18.3% of
R1's in-scope universe**.

Because these are corrections to *their* model, R1's primary net-return figures
use BDW's stated model unchanged, so that any gap against their Figure 5 is
theirs to explain; the sourced schedule is reported as a sensitivity. It moves
the bottom-band net return from −49.16% to −48.77% and leaves the maker ≥50c
margin unchanged.

One gap remains open and is carried as bounds rather than closed by assumption:
from the 2025-10-01 version the document stopped enumerating series, so
membership after that date is propagated through the fee-sensitivity ribbon as
evidence bounds (103 series primary, 138 upper).

The consequence for the design is larger than the numbers. A step dummy at one
exchange-wide date is the wrong estimator for a treatment that touched a
minority of markets, was revised five times, and whose intensity ran 5.5% →
9.4% → 17.6% → 14.5% → 32.0% → 33.5% before decaying. That is why the fee
question moved to a difference-in-differences.

## 5. R2: does the bias persist?

The primary estimands are the two interaction coefficients from a single
pooled, category-interacted Mincer–Zarnowitz regression, with boundaries at the
maker fee (2025-05-01) and publication (2025-09-08), event-clustered standard
errors, and headline aggregates weighted by the **frozen calendar-2024 category
mix** — the last full pre-sports year. Sports consequently carries essentially
zero weight in the headline and is reported as its own stratum. That is the
design, not a limitation of it.

The pooled panel is **1,330,445 observations** (124,732 from R1, 1,205,713 from
R2) across 17 categories, with ψ̄_R1 = 0.0254.

| | δ̄ | 95% CI | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fee | +0.0399 | [+0.0071, +0.0726] | indeterminate |
| Publication | −0.0311 | [−0.0637, +0.0014] | indeterminate |

Both verdicts are "indeterminate", and in both cases that is the pre-registered
vocabulary working rather than failing. The fee interval excludes zero but the
point estimate is *positive* — the bias, measured this way, got stronger — and
none of persisted, attenuated, vanished or reversed describes that. The
publication interval contains both zero and −ψ̄_R1, so persisted and vanished
cannot be distinguished on this sample. The plan's instruction for such cases is
to report them as indeterminate and not force a label.

**The fee question, properly identified.** The series-level DiD compares treated
and untreated series observed in the same calendar months, with month terms
entering the slope as well as the level because the estimand is a slope:

| Specification | δ_did | s.e. | 95% CI |
|---|---|---|---|
| Two-way fixed effects | +0.0113 | 0.0129 | [−0.0139, +0.0365] |
| Clean controls | **−0.0016** | **0.0064** | [−0.0141, +0.0109] |

Estimated on 98 treated series, 141,708 treated observations against 1,188,737
controls, 119,646 event clusters, 60 months, with no cell thin enough to need a
wild cluster bootstrap. Because two-way fixed effects with staggered adoption
lets already-treated units serve as controls for later-treated ones, both fits
are always reported; the clean-controls variant compares treated observations
only against never-treated series, and on disagreement it is the one reported.

It is a tight null. The maker fee did not detectably change the slope.

**Why the two disagree.** The naive δ̄_fee applies a step to a sample in which
most observations were never treated, against a treatment whose intensity
quadrupled and then halved inside the window. Its within component is also
almost entirely one category: Financials contributes +0.0437 of the +0.0399,
on a Δψ of +0.1435, while holding 30.5% of the frozen weight against 0.59% of
the current sample. The frozen mix is behaving exactly as specified — that is
what holding composition fixed means — but the headline consequently rests on a
cell that shrank by a factor of fifty. We report it, and we do not build a
persistence claim on it.

## 6. Composition is most of the naive answer

The decomposition `Δψ_agg = Σ w̄_c·Δψ_c + Σ Δw_c·ψ̄_c` separates within-category
change from between-category composition change. At the fee boundary:

**within +0.0399, between +0.0278, aggregate +0.0677.**

Forty-one percent of the aggregate movement is composition. The driver is not
subtle:

| Category | 2024 weight | R2 weight | between contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sports | 0.00009 | **0.5875** | **+0.0437** |
| Climate & Weather | 0.4744 | 0.0995 | −0.0090 |
| Financials | 0.3047 | 0.0059 | −0.0059 |

Sports launched on Kalshi in early 2025 — almost exactly at the R1/R2 boundary —
and by the end of our window it is 58.8% of the in-scope sample. On its own it
contributes more than the entire between component. Four categories in the R2
window (Exotics, Mentions, Social, Transportation) did not exist in calendar
2024 at all and therefore carry zero headline weight by construction, reported
as their own strata.

This is the note's most portable finding. Kalshi is now a heavily studied
venue, and an aggregate before/after comparison across early 2025 does not
measure a change in how the market prices risk. It measures sports arriving.
Any persistence claim on this venue needs the composition held fixed or
decomposed; ours is the within component, and every narrative sentence in this
note about "the bias" refers to that component only.

## 7. Robustness

**Horizon.** The panel pools eleven lookback horizons. Re-estimated
horizon-by-horizon, δ̄_fee swings from +0.098 (day 1) to −0.008 (day 9), and the
one-observation-per-contract closing-price specification gives **+0.0117**
against the pooled +0.0399. The pre-registered test is that a δ surviving both
is not horizon-composition drift. This one does not survive cleanly, which is a
further reason not to read the naive fee coefficient as a behavioural result.

**The maker margin and its fee-sensitivity ribbon.** The margin at prices ≥50c
is computed in three fee layers on 202,725,609 maker and 167,925,545 taker
sides, with zero observations lost to gaps in the fee history:

| Layer | Margin |
|---|---|
| (a) gross | +2.40% |
| (b) net of own-era fees | +4.39% |
| (c) pre-2025 schedule held constant | +4.54% |

Layer (b) exceeding layer (a) is the expected direction rather than an error:
under fees the taker pays and the maker mostly does not, so the maker–taker
spread widens. Swept across an eleven-point grid spanning the plausible maker
fee band, the margin falls monotonically from +0.0454 to +0.0431 and **never
crosses zero**. There is no break-even rate inside the band and the result is
not labelled fragile.

So BDW's headline exploitable margin is still there after the boundary, and no
plausible maker fee erases it.

**Control venue.** Polymarket's monthly slope over 2025-05 to 2025-12 serves as
a secular-trend check, not a difference-in-differences. Three caveats are stated
here rather than left for a referee: Polymarket's tail bias is *reversed*
relative to Kalshi's, so this controls for market-wide efficiency drift and not
for level or sign, and parallel-trends language is off the table; the archive's
provenance is disclosed; and cross-venue arbitrage could in principle propagate
BDW's publication to Polymarket too, which would strengthen rather than
undermine a secular-trend reading.

The control covers 2025-05 through 2025-12 only, and this is structural rather
than a collection gap: Polymarket's own staggered 2026 fee reform would
contaminate any longer archive with Polymarket's own treatment. δ_fee is
unaffected, since its identification is now within-Kalshi. **δ_pub is
controlled only through 2025-12-31**, and the remaining six months are reported
as an uncontrolled extension of the horizon, never averaged across it.

**Escalation.** The pre-registered rule escalates to a standalone paper only if
the fee arm rejects zero in both DiD fits, or δ̄_pub rejects zero, or the maker
≥50c margin changes sign between layers (a) and (c) and survives the ribbon.
None fires. This note is the appropriate format, and that was decided by the
rule as committed.

## 8. Related work

BDW remains a working paper as of this draft (January 2026 version; CEPR DP
20631, CESifo WP 12122, UCD WP2025_19, GWU WP 2026-001, MPRA 126350). Journal
status should be re-checked at submission.

Whelan (2023) introduces fees into a prediction-market model and shows that fees
charged on winnings generate a form of favorite–longshot bias in post-fee loss
rates. It is theoretical and uses no Kalshi data; our reconstruction of the
actual schedule speaks directly to its assumptions, since the real fee turns out
to be neither uniform nor, initially, price-dependent.

Becker (2026) is the closest empirical work. It analyses 72.1 million Kalshi
trades over June 2021 to November 2025, confirms the longshot bias by price
level, decomposes returns by market role — takers −1.12% and makers +1.12% mean
excess return per trade — and documents a YES/NO asymmetry in taker order flow.
Its maker/taker finding is consistent with ours in direction; the magnitudes are
not comparable because the estimand differs (excess return per trade versus
return on a contract position). Becker does not analyse the fee regime, does not
test persistence at dated boundaries, and does not address the composition
confound; its sample also ends seven months before ours. We read its existence
as evidence for this note's Section 6: aggregate analyses of Kalshi across the
2025 boundary are already being produced.

## 9. Conclusion

BDW asked whether the biases they documented would persist once documented. On
the estimate that identifies, the answer for the fee treatment is that nothing
detectable happened: −0.0016 with a standard error of 0.0064. The maker's edge
at prices at or above 50c is still present after the boundary and survives every
plausible maker fee rate. For publication, the data cannot distinguish
persistence from disappearance, and we say so rather than picking.

The finding we would most want carried forward is not either coefficient. It is
that 41% of the naive aggregate movement at the fee boundary is one asset class
arriving, and that anyone comparing Kalshi before and after early 2025 without
holding composition fixed will find a large effect that is not there.

## Appendix A — divergences, stated not smoothed

**BDW's 63-contract mismatch filter does not reproduce.** They drop 63 of 46,282
Yes contracts (0.136%) for mismatching Kalshi's separately reported final
prices. All four readings available from Kalshi's public fields were measured
against that rate: a last-trade proxy fires never; tape price versus Kalshi's
`last_price` at ≥1c gives 4.345%, thirty-two times too many; settlement value
versus `result` gives 0.003%, forty-five times too few. The two quantities in
the price reading differ by definition, so a disagreement is not evidence of an
error, and tuning a threshold to land on 63 would fit a filter whose definition
we do not know to a number we do. We implement the one unambiguous data error
instead — Kalshi's settlement value contradicting its own `result`, 1 contract
in 32,728 — retain the contracts BDW dropped, and log the divergence. The
discarded comparison became a validation: **95.7% of our tape-derived closing
prices match Kalshi's independently reported final price to the cent**, with
median, p90 and p95 differences all exactly zero.

**Coverage.** 3,257 markets (8.2% of those clearing volume and duration) have no
retrievable bid/ask history and are structurally lost to the spread filter.
11 markets are unfetched. Neither is fixable by more collection.

## Appendix B — what this design cannot do

This is a specification commitment on historical data, not outcome-blind
pre-registration, and it should not be described as the latter. The
`analysis_plan.md` equations, thresholds and verdict vocabulary were committed
on 2026-07-28 before any R2 estimate was computed, and the frozen category mix
was committed before the estimate that uses it. That is the honest claim.

δ_pub is controlled only through 2025-12-31. Thin category cells are handled
with a wild cluster bootstrap where needed and reported as insufficient
otherwise. The post-2025-10-01 maker-fee series membership is a genuine open
gap, carried as bounds.
